summary: When one server gets overloaded, compare making it bigger with adding more servers.
goals: Recognize the signs that a server is overloaded.
Learn when scaling up helps and where it stops helping.
Learn how scaling out adds capacity with more servers.
See how autoscaling follows regular demand and why sudden spikes need planning.
Understand why more servers need a load balancer.

steps.title: Begin with one server
body: The app runs on one computer. Every request—opening a page or posting a photo—travels from the user’s device to that server and back.
With 100 users, the server has plenty of room. Its CPU is busy only about 1% of the time.
steps.callout: A server has limits for CPU, memory, disk, and network. Its capacity is how much work it can do before one of those resources becomes a limit.

steps.title: A sudden jump in traffic
body: A post becomes popular and traffic grows 120 times. This server can handle about 400 requests each second, but 480 arrive. Its CPU reaches 100%, requests wait in a queue, responses get slow, and some requests time out.
The app needs more capacity. There are two main ways to add it.
steps.callout: Overload often shows up as CPU near 100%, a growing queue, slower responses, and then timeouts.

steps.title: Way 1: scale up
body: Move the app to a bigger computer with more CPU cores, more memory, or faster disks. The app design stays the same, so the code usually needs no changes.
This is vertical scaling, also called scaling up.
steps.callout: Scaling up is often a simple first step: it needs no code changes and adds no new kind of component to operate. A machine with four times the capacity may cost about four times as much.

steps.title: Scaling up has a limit
body: Vertical scaling has a hardware limit. A workload that uses 16 cores well may not use 192 cores as well, because those cores share locks, memory, and a disk. Moving to a bigger machine can require a migration and restart, causing downtime. Large machines can also cost much more, and twice as many cores may not deliver twice as much throughput.
Moving to a new machine can require a restart and a migration, which may cause downtime.
steps.callout: Vertical scaling has a hardware limit. Large machines can also cost much more, and twice as many cores may not deliver twice as much throughput.

steps.title: One server is one point of failure
body: All users depend on this one machine. A bad software release, a full disk, or a power failure can take the whole app offline.
A component whose failure can stop the entire system is a single point of failure (SPOF).
steps.callout: Even the biggest machine can fail. If everything depends on it, one failure can cause a full outage.

steps.title: Way 2: scale out
body: Run several medium-sized computers side by side. In this example, four servers each have 96 vCPUs and run the same app. If more capacity is needed, add another server. Medium-sized machines can offer good value, and there is no single-machine ceiling.
This is horizontal scaling, also called scaling out. Here, four servers provide twice the capacity of the largest single machine. If one fails, the other three can carry the load.
steps.callout: Four medium servers can offer more total capacity than the largest single server. If one fails, the remaining servers may still handle some traffic.

steps.title: Capacity sits unused overnight
body: Traffic changes through the day. At 8 p.m. the app needs all four servers. At 4 a.m. traffic is one tenth as high, and the servers are only 5% busy.
You still pay for peak capacity even when most of it is idle. Consumer apps often see a 3–10× difference between daily peak and quiet hours.
steps.callout: Consumer apps often have daily traffic peaks several times larger than their quiet hours.

steps.title: Let autoscaling follow demand
body: Because the servers can do the same work, an autoscaler can add or remove them based on demand. For example, it can try to keep average CPU use near 50%.
At night it scales in to two servers, keeping one extra in case of a failure. In the evening it scales back out. This reduces the time you pay for unused machines.
steps.callout: Autoscaling works when servers can take requests interchangeably and a load balancer sends traffic to them. The next lessons cover these ideas.

steps.title: Case: a flash sale
body: Two servers are handling traffic comfortably. A flash sale starts, and traffic grows five times in two minutes. The autoscaler starts new servers, but they take about three minutes to start and warm up.
During those minutes, the two existing servers can handle only about two-thirds of the requests. For a planned sale, add capacity before it starts. Keep spare capacity for surprise spikes.
steps.callout: Autoscaling reacts to demand after it appears. For known launches, sales, or broadcasts, start extra servers early.

steps.title: Who sends each user to a server?
body: Suppose each group of users is set up to contact one server directly. If Server B fails, the quarter of users assigned to it see errors—even though three healthy servers remain.
A client does not know which servers are healthy or busy. A component in front of the servers must choose where each request goes.
steps.callout: That component is a load balancer. It sends requests to healthy servers; the next lesson explains how.

steps.title: Recap: scale up or scale out
body:
Scale upScale out
HowBigger machineMore machines
Code changesNoneSome1
CeilingHardware limitPractically none
FailureTotal outagePartial2
To growMigrate + restartAdd a server
CostPremium at the topLinear
Scaling out also lets you autoscale: add servers for the evening peak and remove them at night.
1 Servers must be interchangeable — see Stateless Services. 2 A load balancer can route around failed servers.
steps.callout: A common approach is to scale up while it is simple and affordable, then scale out when one machine is no longer enough.
